title: Modernizing Legacy UX
intro: A legacy product succeeded and then stopped fitting. Modernize when keeping it costs more than it returns, and aim at what should exist now.

learn.title: Legacy is success that no longer fits
learn.text:
Legacy software isn’t bad software. It was right for its time and has drifted from what people need.

**Common failure modes:** late-found dependencies, worn-down people, the **feature-parity trap**, innovation theatre, a feature factory, and delivering too late.

Behind most of them are unknown unknowns that only surface once migration begins.

try.q: Which of these is the feature-parity trap?
options: Requiring the new product to match every old feature
Launching a new look on the same old workflows
Shipping a long feature list without checking it helps
Discovering hidden dependencies in the final month
try.explain: Parity rebuilds every past compromise. The others are innovation theatre, a feature factory and late-found dependencies.

learn.title: Modernize the product, not the interface
learn.text:
Ask **“what should exist now?”** before “what must we carry over?”.

Start with a working group of people who use the legacy product every day. They know which parts are load-bearing and which are just habit.

Multi-year rebuilds often deliver what was needed one to three years ago.

options: With a working group of daily legacy users
With a complete inventory of every old feature
With a visual refresh of the existing screens
With an early retirement date for the old system
try.explain: They can tell you what the old product really does and what no longer matters.

learn.title: Migrate by slice, not by feature
learn.text:
Five common strategies: **big bang**, **incremental**, **parallel** (a public beta), **incremental and parallel** (power users first, once the new version matches the old on day one), and **upgrading the legacy UI** while a new one runs in beta.

Whichever you pick, migrate **one key workflow at a time**, end to end, and pilot each slice with a small group to build trust.

A claim that 65–79% of modernizations fail circulates widely but has no source in the original article. Leave it out of a business case.

try.q: What is the better unit of migration?
options: A key workflow, end to end
A single feature, one at a time
A single screen, one at a time
A single team, one at a time
try.explain: A finished workflow teaches you more than a feature that is only part of a task.

test.q: What best describes a legacy product?
options: Successful software that has stopped fitting
Software that was written in an outdated language
Software that has lost all of its remaining users
Software that nobody maintains any more
test.explain: Legacy is about fit, not age. The product worked, and the needs moved.

test.q: Why do multi-year rebuilds often disappoint?
options: They ship what was needed years ago
Engineers always underestimate the effort
Users dislike every new interface they meet
Old systems cannot be replaced by new ones
test.explain: By the time a long project ships, the needs it was built for have changed.

test.q: Which strategy lets power users move first?
options: Incremental and parallel
Big bang
Upgrading the legacy UI only
A parallel beta open to everyone
test.explain: Power users move first once the new version matches the old on day one.

test.q: Why shouldn’t you quote “65–79% of modernizations fail” in a business case?
options: The source article cites no reference
It is true only for large banks
It counts only big-bang projects
It is more than ten years old
test.explain: A figure without a source can’t be defended when someone asks where it came from.

test.q: Why pilot each slice with a small group?
options: Early wins build trust for later slices
It removes the need for a working group
It means training can be skipped entirely
It lets the team skip usability testing
test.explain: Trust is the scarce resource in a long migration. A pilot earns it one slice at a time.
